extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency officials, policymakers, and lawyers working on notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal-analytical criteria for how agencies should understand, evaluate, and respond to mass, malattributed, and computer-generated public comments in notice-and-comment rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass comment response definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A “mass comment response” will feature at least an order of magnitude increase (e.g., 10x) in the number of comments received vis-à-vis a typical rulemaking for that agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article adopts this working definition based on interviews with agency officials and acknowledges it is somewhat arbitrary; the threshold will vary by agency and rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass comment campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: A special case of a mass comment response in which one or more organizations has successfully urged a large number of individuals or groups to submit comments to the agency or has submitted comments in their names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass campaigns often produce identical or nearly identical language (sample comments), may encourage minor personalization, and can be difficult to distinguish from spontaneous mass responses when submissions are unique but substantively similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments falsely attributed to persons who did not in fact submit them (false names or submissions made without the purported submitter's awareness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technologies and large datasets (e.g., DMV or voter registration data) and automation make malattribution easier and able to occur at scale; terminology includes 'fraudulent', 'fake', 'pseudonymous', 'fabricated', 'inauthentic', and 'misattributed'. The Article focuses on false identity specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments generated by a software algorithm that replace human content generation and interaction with the agency; once automated, software can submit comments (even repeatedly) without further human engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While early bot comments were crude, advances in NLP (e.g., GPT-3) make human-quality automated comments increasingly possible. Computer-generated comments could overwhelm agencies, but they can also offer beneficial, narrowly technical uses (e.g., reporting spelling errors, drafting assistance). Agencies should be cautious about overly restrictive responses that would preclude useful technical tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information quality — technical/operational information
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical or operational information (scientific/engineering studies, data, analysis of how a regulatory change addresses a problem, compliance costs, legal or policy analysis) is the most useful type of information agencies may obtain from comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such information empowers agency decisionmakers to anticipate consequences and contributes to higher-quality, technically proficient rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information quality — preference information and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of preference (views about desirability of a rule) have contested relevance: some scholars argue they are inappropriate for technical deliberation, while others argue agencies should sometimes consider preferences when statutes leave values unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article summarizes the scholarly debate (e.g., Farina vs. Mendelson) and notes concerns about representativeness of preference signals derived from comment pools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and judicial limits on what agencies may consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies cannot rely on factors Congress did not intend them to consider; some statutes leave no room for public sentiment on particular matters (State Farm formulation; Whitman example: EPA cannot consider costs when setting NAAQS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have invalidated agency reliance on inappropriate factors; agencies must be vigilant about statutory constraints when assessing comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance/materiality threshold for comments (HBO/Portland Cement standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only comments which, if true, raise points relevant to the agency’s decision and which, if adopted, would require a change in an agency’s proposed rule are significant; purely speculative comments that do not disclose factual or policy bases require no response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require that comments 'step over a threshold requirement of materiality' or 'challenge a fundamental premise' before an agency must respond; this standard is drawn from D.C. Circuit precedent (Home Box Office; Portland Cement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency obligation to respond in a reasoned manner
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must respond 'in a reasoned manner' to the comments it receives, explaining how it resolved significant problems raised by the comments and showing how that resolution led to the ultimate rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no obligation to answer every submission; failure to respond is problematic only if it demonstrates the agency's decision was not based on consideration of relevant factors (citing Action on Smoking & Health and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical volume is not dispositive ('not a vote')
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are under no obligation to adopt the approach advocated by the largest number of commenters; the public comment process is not a vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have repeatedly emphasized that sheer numbers do not by themselves compel a change in agency action and have deemphasized the weight of comment counts in judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing costs and resource-burden consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Large volumes of comments increase time and resource costs to review, analyze, and respond, sometimes requiring contractors or substantial staff time; identification of malattributed or computer-generated comments further increases costs and delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comment-derived information is valuable, processing costs may be justified, but the financial and delay costs of spurious or low-quality comments are nontrivial and relevant to agencies' responses and resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive legitimacy and procedural fairness elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive (sociological) legitimacy of agency decisionmaking depends in part on perceived procedural fairness; three key process elements are voice, polite and respectful treatment, and explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice-and-comment maps to the 'voice' element; mass, malattributed, or computer-generated comments may undermine public confidence in the ability to be heard or in procedural fairness even if agencies can technically sort through the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of misinformation and falsehoods
rubrics_metrics.description: False or erroneous statements in comments (intentional or not) can distract agency reviewers, delay processing, and, if undiscovered and material, negatively affect the substance of a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency expertise and broad participation can mitigate misinformation (expert staff recognize errors; true submissions may counter false ones), but misinformation remains a growing concern for e-rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness concerns and intermediary influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comment responses raise questions about the representativeness of commenters and the role of intermediary organizations that solicit or coordinate large numbers of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies might pay attention to volume to gauge public resistance, but intermediaries that orchestrate campaigns (post templates, encourage verbatim submission) complicate assessments of representativeness and genuine public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detectability and differentiation challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishing bot-generated, malattributed, or machine-generated comments from genuine human submissions can be difficult—particularly as NLP and AI advance to produce human-like text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier computer-generated comments were crude and easier to detect, but contemporary language models produce outputs that are harder to distinguish; the Article notes experiments and the risk that high-quality automated comments could overwhelm agencies.
